title: The "Alien Megastructure" Star Is Still Unexplained 15 Years Later, and a Giant Planet Is Now Among the Suspects

content:
A star 1,470 light-years away dims irregularly, by as much as 22%. Volunteer amateurs found it, headlines floated alien megastructures, and no single explanation covers everything observed. Now a possible giant planet, and a rival idea from Tenerife, are on the table.

In 2011, an amateur astronomer near Toronto, Adam Szewczyk, was going through star brightness charts at home when one caught his eye. He left a comment on a forum for volunteers: there was an odd dip, something like a giant transit, the term for a planet crossing in front of its star and blocking a sliver of its light.

The other participants noted it with mild interest and filed it away as one more oddity. Two years later the same star suddenly lost more than a fifth of its light, and the curiosity became one of the most discussed puzzles in recent astronomy.

Today the star has three nicknames (Tabby’s Star, Boyajian’s Star and the WTF Star), several explanations that each cover part of what we see, and none that covers all of it. Its dips in brightness have even been named after ancient cities such as Skara Brae and Angkor, and in summer 2026 a possible giant planet entered the picture. Let’s take it step by step.

An ordinary star behaving strangely

For almost two thousand years, the dominant idea in the West, inherited from Aristotle, was that the heavens were perfect and unchanging. It began to crack in 1572, when Tycho Brahe saw a “new star” in the constellation Cassiopeia.

In 1596 a Protestant pastor, David Fabricius, noticed that another star, in the constellation Cetus (the Whale), faded and returned over time. We call it Mira today, and it is usually considered the first variable star ever identified.

A star that changes brightness is therefore nothing unusual. Some pulsate, some spin with giant spots, some come in pairs that eclipse each other, and almost all follow a pattern that lets astronomers make sense of them. This one doesn’t.

Its official name is KIC 8462852, from the catalogue of NASA’s Kepler mission, and it lies in the constellation Cygnus, the Swan, about 1,470 light-years from Earth. It is an F-type star, a little bigger than the Sun and about 1,000 degrees hotter.

It also has a distant companion, a red dwarf (a small, cool star) roughly 30 times farther from it than Neptune is from the Sun, and the two were confirmed as relatives in 2021. The star is too faint for the naked eye, but a telescope of about 5 inches (13 cm) under a dark sky is enough to find it.

The light Kepler recorded in 2011 left that star around the year 540. Justinian had just opened the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, and Teudis ruled the Visigoths in Spain. The probe Voyager 1, one of the fastest craft we have ever launched, would need about 26 million years to cover the same distance.

Kepler watched more than 150,000 stars for four years, measuring each one’s brightness every half hour. It was hunting for transits, the small dimming a planet causes when it passes in front of its star, and it logged them on a light curve, which is simply a graph of brightness over time.

A Jupiter-sized planet blocks less than 1% of the light of a star like this one. KIC 8462852 fell by 15% on March 5, 2011, and by 22% on February 28, 2013, with smaller dips in between. They were neither regular nor symmetrical, and they lasted anywhere from about five days to nearly three months.

The volunteers who caught what the algorithm threw away

Kepler produced billions of data points a year, and its software was built to keep only what looked like a planet and discard the rest, as Jason Wright of Penn State has explained. To rescue the oddities, a Yale University team led by Debra Fischer created Planet Hunters, a citizen-science project where anyone can inspect 30-day stretches of light curves by eye.

Szewczyk was the first to comment on that dip. Daryll LaCourse, a veteran who reckons he has classified tens of thousands of curves, noticed that the drop was lopsided, unlike the symmetrical shape of a textbook transit.

They wrote to Tabetha Boyajian, then a postdoctoral researcher at Yale who acted as the link with the volunteers. Her first thought, like any professional astronomer’s, was a data glitch. But the volunteers had already run the checks that catch faulty data, and the signal was real.

The paper carried 49 authors, 11 of them amateurs (LaCourse was second on the list). It appeared on arXiv, the open site where scientists post drafts, in September 2015, and the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society published it in 2016.

To gather data, Boyajian had called in favors around the world, including time on a telescope at the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory on La Palma. The conclusions were unsatisfying. The star was an ordinary F-type, no extra heat from hot dust showed up, and nearly every explanation they tried failed.

The best fit was a family of exocomets (comets orbiting another star), fragments of a single body that had broken up long ago.

Aliens, always the last hypothesis

On October 13, 2015, journalist Ross Andersen published a report in The Atlantic titled “The Most Mysterious Star in Our Galaxy”. Wright said there that he and colleagues were preparing a paper arguing the light curve was compatible with a swarm of megastructures built by an advanced civilization.

The idea goes back to a 1960 proposal by physicist Freeman Dyson. A civilization hungry for energy could surround its star with solar collectors and harvest a large share of its light, a concept popularly known as a Dyson sphere.

Wright was cautious. Aliens, he said, should always be the last hypothesis anyone considers, though this did resemble what you might expect from a civilization of builders.

His paper, with Kimberly Cartier, Ming Zhao, Daniel Jontof-Hutter and Eric Ford, reached arXiv on October 15, 2015, and proposed the star as a top target in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. Steve Howell, NASA’s Kepler scientist, thought jumping to aliens was overblown. The checks were made anyway.

The SETI Institute pointed the Allen Telescope Array in California at the star for two weeks and found no artificial radio signals. That rules out transmitters broadcasting in all directions with about a hundred times the energy humanity uses today, although something more modest, or beamed at us, would have slipped past.

Later searches for flashes of light, including a laser survey in 2018 whose candidates turned out to be of earthly origin, have found nothing either.

A century of data and an argument that won’t close

In January 2016, astronomer Bradley Schaefer published an analysis of about 1,300 photographic plates from the Harvard Observatory taken between 1890 and 1989. By his reckoning the star had faded by around 16% in a hundred years, something unheard of for a star of its kind.

A few months later, a team led by Michael Hippke repeated the exercise with plates from the Sonneberg Observatory in Germany and concluded that the brightness had stayed constant to within 3%, which is incompatible with Schaefer’s drop.

What does look real is a slow fading during Kepler’s own mission. Benjamin Montet and Joshua Simon went back to the full images the spacecraft took each month and found that the star lost about 3% of its brightness over four years. None of 193 neighboring stars did the same, nor did 355 stars with similar characteristics.

Given those results, Wright and astronomer Steinn Sigurðsson concluded that same year that there was no good explanation for either the abrupt dips or the slow trend. Whether the century-long dimming is real or an artifact of the old plates remains an open question.

Elsie, Skara Brae and Angkor: dust that isn’t opaque

Catching the next dip live required telescopes available every night, which professional observatories can’t offer, since their time is handed out months in advance. Boyajian and Wright turned to the network of the Las Cumbres Observatory and to Kickstarter. In 2016, more than 1,700 people contributed over $100,000.

The alert came in May 2017. The star began to dim, and dozens of telescopes were pointed at it within hours. The backers got to name the dips. The first was Elsie, from how “LC” sounds when spoken, the initials of light curve and of Las Cumbres. Celeste, Skara Brae and Angkor followed, the last two named after ancient cities.

Skara Brae is a Neolithic village in Scotland’s Orkney Islands, occupied from about 3180 to 2500 BC and uncovered by a storm in 1850. Angkor is the great abandoned capital of Cambodia. In 2018 came Caral-Supe, the Peruvian city some 5,000 years old, and Evangeline.

What mattered most for science was the color of each dip. A solid, opaque object, such as a planet or an artificial structure, blocks all colors equally. Very fine dust does something different, and the closest everyday example is a sunset, when the air scatters blue light first and the Sun looks reddish. The 2017 observations, published in 2018 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters by Boyajian and more than two hundred coauthors, showed that the dips were deeper in blue than in red.

The Gran Telescopio Canarias, also on La Palma, gave independent confirmation. Hans Deeg, Roi Alonso and David Nespral, of the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias, followed the star with Boyajian on 16 occasions between May and December 2017 and reached the same conclusion.

What blocked the light was tiny particles, smaller than a thousandth of a millimeter and far thinner than a human hair. Wright later summed it up: explanations relying only on opaque objects (planets, stars, swarms of asteroids or megastructures) were ruled out.

The question still stood, though. Where does that dust come from, and why isn’t the heat it should give off showing up?

Comets, a swallowed planet and orphaned moons

Several answers have circulated since, and none is airtight. The exocomet idea came first, and in 2016 Eva Bodman and Alice Quillen modeled the swarms that would be needed to reproduce the light curve. Other researchers have pointed out that so many comets are hard to justify, and that the shape of some dips, a gentle descent followed by an abrupt recovery, fits them badly.

Another team proposed that the star swallowed a planet long ago, leaving clouds of debris on stretched-out orbits. In 2019, two papers turned to moons. Mario Sucerquia, of the Universidad de Antioquia in Colombia, and colleagues simulated what happens to the large moons of giant planets that migrate toward their star.

Moons that break free (“ploonets”) could, they suggested, produce light curves like this one. Miguel Martínez, Nicholas Stone and Brian Metzger argued that an “orphan” moon evaporating near the star would leave enough dust. Some researchers look inside the star itself, at changes in how it carries heat. None of these ideas explains everything on its own.

2026: a possible giant planet and a reading from Tenerife

On September 3, 2019, NASA’s TESS satellite, built to search for planets around nearby stars, recorded a dip unlike any before it. It lasted about 21 hours, took roughly 1% of the light and was symmetrical, like a textbook transit.

Astronomer Cristina Madurga Favieres spotted it. A doctoral student at the University of Warwick in the UK, trained at the Complutense University of Madrid, she signs the analysis with British and French colleagues. It was published in summer 2026 in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, with a draft on arXiv since July 22.

The team combined those data with radial velocity measurements, a method that picks up the gravitational tug of a massive body on its star through tiny shifts in the color of its light. They used observations from several telescopes, among them the Nordic Optical Telescope on La Palma.

The result points to a companion about nine times the mass of Jupiter, halfway between a giant planet and a brown dwarf, an object too big to be a planet and too small to be a star. Its orbit would take at least nearly three years, at a distance similar to our solar system’s asteroid belt.

The authors themselves call it a tentative hint, because the mass signal is far from the level of certainty needed to call a discovery confirmed. If the companion exists, it would help explain the arrival of comets, since its gravity would steer them toward the star. According to the paper, comet models also fit the TESS dip poorly.

Wright, however, was skeptical on Bluesky on July 25. He said the paper’s radial velocity measurements don’t show a planet or brown dwarf on their own and, at most, rule out giant companions at various orbital periods, leaving only a narrow range of possibilities.

From the Canary Islands comes a different reading of the same data. Héctor Socas-Navarro, a researcher at the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias and director of the European Solar Telescope Foundation, posted a draft on arXiv on September 2 that other scientists have not yet reviewed.

He asks whether the fact that individual dips never repeat is hiding something else, namely that groups of dips do. His proposal is that a planetary body broke apart shortly before the big 2011 dip, and that its fragments, on slightly different orbits, spread a little further apart with each lap.

By his analysis, the timing of those groups fits a cycle of just over two years much better than it fits pure chance. He is careful to add that this result depends on the model’s assumptions and is not proof.

In his scenario, which he calls Alderaan (the name echoes the planet destroyed in Star Wars), the object that crossed the star in 2019 would not be a giant planet but the largest remnant of that broken body. He admits to one striking coincidence, which is that Kepler would have caught an apparently mature system within days of a major breakup.

The answer could come as early as December. According to EarthSky, the next data release from the Gaia satellite, which measures the positions of stars with enormous precision, is scheduled for that month, and the authors of the TESS paper hope its measurements will clarify what the object is.

If Gaia detects the wobble a massive companion would cause, the star has a planet that stirs up comets. If it doesn’t, Socas-Navarro’s reading, with a broken body and its debris, gains ground, or perhaps a third explanation will appear. Today nobody can say what is blocking the star’s light, or even whether there is only one cause.
